# C6. The cross-country test {#esc-oecd26}

Section {{< var p.sec_esc >}} of the paper ends with a test of the model across the OECD countries of figure
{{< var p.fig_US_OECDdata >}}. The U.S., measured as the other countries are, from the OECD earnings deciles at the
U.S. income percentiles, anchors the test: its political weight of the old ω and its cost parameter λ. Layer 1
gives every other country the U.S. ω and λ with its own workers per retiree, income distribution and observed
design, and predicts its tax rate and its design. Layer 2 calibrates each country's ω to its pension spending and
predicts its design. The model's design is the one in force in 2020, chosen in 1990, as for the U.S. target of λ.
The paper leaves out the countries whose informal employment is high and gives every country the U.S. propensities
to vote by income group. This page repeats the test with all the countries of the figure, and with each country's
own propensities to vote.

## All the countries {#esc-oecd26-all}

Korea, Mexico and Turkey join the sample. The data's slope of spending on the Gini then turns negative, the
model's sign, and the data's slope of the index on population growth flattens toward layer 1's. The other signs
are those on the paper's sample: spending falls with population growth and rises with the index in the data and
in the model, the model's spending rising more steeply with the index; the index falls with population growth in
the data and in both layers; and the index rises with the Gini in the data, not significantly, where it falls in
both layers. The table after the slopes gives the political weight of the old each country's spending implies.

## Each country's own turnout {#esc-oecd26-turnout}

Each country's propensities to vote by income group now come from the CSES. The U.S. anchor is recalibrated at
its own CSES turnout, which raises λ, and Luxembourg, with no CSES election, leaves data and model alike. The
relations the test reproduces at the U.S. turnout keep their signs: spending falls with population growth, about as
steeply in layer 1 as in the data on these countries, and rises with the index in both layers, and the index falls
with population growth in both layers. On the Gini, where the data show no significant relation, layer 1's slope of the
index nearly vanishes and layer 2's takes the data's sign, neither significantly, while layer 1's slope of
spending keeps the sign opposite to the data's.
